result.summary: The Chorus pities Prometheus, then the cow-horned Io arrives, driven mad by a gad-fly sent by Hera. She tells her story, and Prometheus foretells her wanderings to Egypt, her descendants, and the hero who will free him. Io is seized again by frenzy.

scenes.title: The Chorus pities Prometheus
scenes.summary: The Chorus prays to avoid Zeus's anger and warns Prometheus that helping mortals was futile.
scenes.stakes: Prometheus suffers endless torture; the Chorus fears offending Zeus.

scenes.title: Io arrives, tormented
scenes.summary: Io, horned and stung by a gad-fly, enters and begs to know who Prometheus is and what awaits her.
scenes.stakes: Io is driven by madness and hunger and cannot escape Hera's persecution.

scenes.title: Prometheus agrees to speak
scenes.summary: Prometheus identifies himself and is reluctant, but the Chorus asks first to hear Io's story.
scenes.stakes: Prometheus hesitates to crush Io's heart with knowledge of her fate.

scenes.title: Io tells her story
scenes.summary: Io recounts the dreams, Inachus' oracles, her exile, her transformation, and Argus' pursuit.
scenes.stakes: Io was cast out by her father under threat of Zeus's thunderbolt.

scenes.title: Io's wanderings foretold
scenes.summary: Prometheus describes Io's route through Scythia, Caucasus, the Amazons and the Bosporus into Asia.
scenes.stakes: Io faces hostile peoples and endless wandering.

scenes.title: Zeus's downfall hinted
scenes.summary: Prometheus hints that Zeus will fall through a marriage, and that a descendant of Io will free him.
scenes.stakes: Prometheus's torment lasts until Zeus falls.

scenes.title: Road to Egypt and descendants
scenes.summary: Prometheus tells of the Gorgons, gryphons, the Nile, Io's past course, Epaphus, the Danaids and the archer who will free him; Io is seized by madness.
scenes.stakes: Io remains tormented until reaching Egypt.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Apollo as god of oracles.

notable_quotes.reason: Prometheus declares his torment lasts until Zeus is overthrown.
Io calls dissembling words the foulest of plagues.

analysis.text: Io's suffering shows the cost of Zeus's arbitrary power, strengthening the play's portrait of tyranny and Prometheus's defiance.
The geographic tour reflects Greek knowledge of distant lands, and explains place names such as Bosporus and Ionian Sea through Io's journey.

legacy.text: The aetiologies of the Bosporus (ox-passage) and Ionian Sea from Io's wandering became standard in Greek tradition.

fun_facts.text: Bosporus means roughly 'ox-ford', which the play links to Io as a cow.

language_notes.text: The Chorus prays not to oppose Zeus and to keep honoring the gods with sacrifice; 'my sire' is Oceanus, father of these sea-nymphs.
'Bootless' means useless or without profit; 'boon' is a favor or gift, here fire and skills given to humans.
'Succour' means help or relief; 'creatures of a day' means short-lived mortals.
'Purblind' means dim-sighted, here suggesting humans' limited understanding.
Refers to the Chorus's earlier wedding song for Prometheus and Hesione, daughter of Oceanus; the mood now contrasts sadly with that song.
Argus was the hundred-eyed giant set by Hera to guard Io; Hermes killed him. His ghost now haunts Io, and the gad-fly is his phantom.
Myriad-eyed means having countless eyes, describing Argus the herdsman.
The wax-compacted pipe is the panpipe of reeds joined with wax; Hermes lulled Argus to sleep with such music.
Son of Cronus is Zeus, who desired Io and whose affair caused Hera's persecution; Io wrongly thinks Prometheus's fate shows Zeus's cruelty.
Disciplined here means punished or taught by suffering; perforce means by compulsion, against her will.
"Fain" means eager or glad; "fain to know" means eager to know.
"Vouchsafe this boon" means to graciously grant this favour.
Hephaestus, the smith god, physically chained Prometheus on Zeus's orders, as the opening scene of the play shows.
"I am nothing loath" means I am not at all unwilling; he fears only the pain the knowledge will cause.
"Sisters of thy sire" means the Chorus of Oceanids are daughters of Oceanus, so they are Io's father's sisters, her aunts.
Lerna was a marshy district near Argos, home to Inachus' pastures; Io's family lived in the Argive region.
Pytho is Delphi, seat of Apollo's oracle; Dodona in Epirus held the oracle of Zeus. Inachus consults both.
Loxias is a title of Apollo, god of Delphic prophecy, whose oracle Inachus obeys.
Gad-fly: a stinging fly that torments cattle, sent to drive Io, now part cow, in frenzy.
Argus, the many-eyed giant herdsman, was set by Hera to guard Io; he was later killed by Hermes.
Cozen means to cheat or deceive; dissembling means disguising the truth.
"Avaunt" is an archaic cry meaning "go away!", here an exclamation of horror at what has been heard.
"Wattled houses on strong-wheeled wains" means huts of woven branches built on sturdy wagons, the mobile homes of nomadic Scythians.
Hybristes means "the violent" or "insolent" in Greek (from hybris), so the river lives up to its name. The footnote marks this pun.
Salmydessus was a rocky Black Sea coast in Thrace, notorious for wrecking ships. Themiscyra on the Thermodon was the legendary Amazon homeland.
Bosporus means "cow's ford" or "cow-passage" in Greek, recalling Io, who is transformed into a heifer.
"Not even reached the prelude" means the sufferings so far are only the beginning of what remains to come.
"Dost" is the archaic second-person singular of "do"; the line means "Do you cry out and groan yet again?"
Prometheus says Io could hardly endure his agonies, since she is mortal. He is immortal and cannot die, so death cannot end his pain.
"I trow" is archaic for "I believe" or "I suppose".
"Empty-headed purposes" means foolish, ill-considered plans; Zeus's own folly will bring about his fall.
"Ruth" means sorrow or regret; the marriage will bring Zeus grief.
"Consort" means spouse; Io asks whether Zeus will be overthrown through his own marriage.
"Mightier than his sire" means stronger than his father. The unnamed son would do to Zeus what Zeus did to Cronus.
"Loose" means untie or set free; "thee" is the archaic singular "you."
Cryptic: the deliverer is a descendant of Io, thirteen generations on in the traditional reading (Heracles). Io cannot yet decode it.
"Purport" means meaning or substance.
"Proffer me a boon" means offer me a favour.
"Fain" means eager or gladly.
"Ye art" is a translator's mixing of plural "ye" with singular "art"; Prometheus addresses Io and the Chorus together.

context_notes.text: The Chorus consists of the daughters of Oceanus, sea-nymphs who come to sympathize with the chained Prometheus.
Prometheus defied Zeus by stealing fire and giving it to humans, which is why he is punished.
Io, daughter of Inachus, was loved by Zeus and turned into a cow by him or Hera; here she has horns and is driven by a gad-fly.
Prometheus is chained to a crag in the Caucasus as punishment from Zeus for giving fire to mankind.
Hera, Zeus's wife, jealously persecutes Io, sending the gad-fly to drive her ceaselessly across the world.
Prometheus, a Titan, stole fire for humans against Zeus's wishes. This is the reason for his punishment.
Io is a maiden turned into a cow and driven by a gadfly across the world, because of Zeus's pursuit and Hera's jealousy.
Zeus desires Io; in the myth Hera's jealousy causes Io's transformation into a cow and her persecution.
Inachus is Io's father, a river-god and king of Argos. Zeus's threat forces him to cast out his own daughter.
Hera, wife of Zeus, persecutes Io, her husband's beloved, by turning her into a cow and sending a gadfly to torment her.
The Chalybes were a people of the Black Sea region famed in antiquity as ironworkers.
The Amazons were a legendary nation of warrior women who shunned men.
Prometheus was chained to a rock by Zeus for giving fire to mankind. He knows a prophecy about Zeus's fall, which he uses as a bargaining secret.
Io, a mortal woman loved by Zeus, was turned into a cow by his jealous wife Hera and driven across the world by a gadfly.
Prometheus knows a secret about Zeus's fall and withholds it as leverage. He is chained to a rock for giving fire to mortals.
Io, a maiden loved by Zeus and turned into a cow-maiden by Hera's jealousy, is driven in endless wandering. Her line leads to Heracles.

literary_notes.text: The question stresses the futility of trusting humans, implying mortals can offer Prometheus no help.
Human weakness is likened to a dream and to being shackled, echoing Prometheus's own chains.
The joyful wedding song is set against the present sorrowful strain, underlining how Prometheus's fortunes have fallen.
The gad-fly is called Argus's phantom, turning an insect's sting into the haunting presence of her dead guardian.
Io cries out to Earth as though it could hear and protect her, showing her desperation.
The earth is said to conceal or refuse to conceal Argus in death, as if it could shelter or betray him.
Her wish for fire, burial or sea monsters shows how extreme her suffering is and how desperate her mind has become.
He names himself by his deed, the gift of fire, defining him as a defiant benefactor of humanity.
Prometheus's warning that ignorance is better hints that Io's coming sufferings are grim.
Prometheus justifies the Chorus's request with a maxim about sympathetic tears, even as he is a bound sufferer who seems to have little need of such consolation.
Calamity as a 'storm' that 'swooped' upon her pictures suffering as a violent natural force falling from above.
The piled-up adjectives 'riddling, obscure, darkly worded' mirror the confusion of the oracles and the family's helplessness.
Inachus obeys the gods' command in seeking their favour, yet the obedience means expelling his own child, 'against his will and mine.'
Io's blunt demand for truth shows her hard-won dignity and sets her honesty against Prometheus's coming revelations.
Grief striking the soul is likened to a double-pronged goad, the tool used to drive cattle, which suits Io's later cow-form and torment.
The river's violent name is said to be fitting, so its character matches its label; a grim wordplay warning Io of danger.
Prometheus appeals to the Chorus to condemn Zeus, whom he calls a tyrant, reinforcing his bitterness toward the new ruler.
The claim that this is not even the prelude warns of far worse suffering ahead, sustaining dread.
Future suffering is imagined as a stormy sea, suggesting it is vast, violent and impossible to escape.
The vague mention of a ruinous marriage hints at Zeus's eventual downfall without naming the bride.
Prometheus answers with a question, withholding the secret. This heightens suspense and shows his control over what Zeus fears.
The all-powerful Zeus depends for his survival on the very prisoner he punishes.
The promise of a descendant of Io as liberator hints at Heracles' coming and the eventual resolution of Prometheus' suffering.
Prometheus' warning that knowledge brings pain heightens Io's, and the audience's, desire to hear more.
